Session Overview Participants swapped stories about working in and dining at restaurants, including tales of generous and demanding customers, unexpectedly high food prices, and being turned away for dress code violations. The group debated whether they qualified as ‘regulars’ anywhere and discussed favorite snacks and ice cream flavors from different cultures. The conversation wrapped up with a lively exchange about exercise habits and whether different activities really require different shoes.
💬 Idioms “crappy day” An informal way to describe a very bad or unpleasant day.
She came home exhausted and barely spoke — it had clearly been a crappy day. Everyone has a crappy day now and then, but a good meal usually helps. “revive (someone’s) faith in humanity” To restore hope or positive feelings about people after a discouraging or frustrating experience.
The stranger who returned her lost wallet really revived her faith in humanity. After so many rude customers, the one generous tipper revived the whole team’s faith in humanity. “fell off the map” To disappear from public attention or become much less popular or active than before.
That ice cream brand was hugely popular a few years ago, but it fell off the map after a product recall. The restaurant opened with great buzz and then fell off the map within a year. “double standard” A situation where a rule is applied fairly to one group but unfairly differently to another.
It is a double standard to require staff to arrive on time but let managers come in late. He felt it was a double standard that women could wear casual shoes inside but men could not. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember regular (noun) — A customer who visits the same place frequently and is well known by the staff there. The barista already knew her order by heart because she was a regular at the café. markup — The amount added to the cost of producing something to arrive at its selling price. The markup on bottled water at concerts is enormous — you pay five times the store price. dress code — An official set of rules stating what clothing is acceptable in a particular place. The club had a strict dress code: no shorts, no flip-flops, and no sleeveless shirts. liability — Legal responsibility for accidents, injuries, or damages that occur in a place or situation. The gym asked members to sign a waiver to limit the gym’s liability in case of injury. dissipate — To gradually spread out and fade away until no longer noticeable (used for smells, smoke, heat, etc.). Open the windows after cooking and the smell of fried food will dissipate quickly. hydrate — To drink enough water or fluids to keep the body properly supplied with moisture. When running outdoors in summer, it is important to hydrate before, during, and after your workout. jerky — Dried, salted, and cured meat cut into strips and eaten as a portable, high-protein snack. He packed beef jerky and nuts for the hiking trip because they do not need refrigeration. tasty — Having a pleasant, enjoyable flavor. (Do not confuse with ’tasteful,’ which means having good aesthetic judgment, not good flavor.) The dried mango she brought was surprisingly tasty — sweet, chewy, and not too sticky. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ I will ask the hot water ✅ I will ask for hot water 💡 Use ‘ask for’ + noun when making a request; ‘ask’ alone needs a person as its object or a ’to’ infinitive ❌ Dried mango is very tasteful ✅ Dried mango is very tasty 💡 ‘Tasteful’ means showing good aesthetic or artistic sense; use ’tasty’ to describe delicious food ❌ Some kind of customers asking me for a lot of requests ✅ Some customers make a lot of requests 💡 Drop ‘kind of’ when speaking generally about a group; ‘make requests’ is the natural collocation — not ‘ask for requests’ ❌ This kind of customer didn’t take well ✅ This kind of customer didn’t tip well 💡 The verb for leaving a gratuity at a restaurant is ’tip,’ not ’take’ ❌ I never do it again ✅ I never did it again 💡 Use simple past (‘did’) for completed past actions, not simple present (‘do’) ❌ At least one times a month ✅ At least once a month 💡 ‘Once’ is the standard English word for one occurrence per time period; ‘one times’ is not natural ❌ when I was very younger, I didn’t eat the eggplant ✅ When I was younger, I didn’t eat eggplant 💡 Comparatives like ‘younger’ do not need ‘very’; also omit the article before food nouns used in a general sense ❌ How much percentage of guest, client? Do they revisit your restaurant? ✅ What percentage of your customers come back regularly? 💡 Use ‘what percentage’ for a proportion question; ‘customers’ is the standard word for people who visit a business ✅ Check Yourself Q1. After a long week of difficult news, one small act of kindness from a stranger was enough to ____.
revive our faith in humanity fell off the map double standard Show answerrevive our faith in humanity — This phrase means to restore hope in people's goodness; 'fell off the map' means to disappear from attention, and 'double standard' is a noun describing unfair rule-applying
Q2. That once-popular sandwich chain had a loyal following, but it ____ after a big food-safety scandal.
fell off the map dissipate hydrate Show answerfell off the map — 'Fell off the map' means to vanish from public attention; 'dissipate' describes a smell or heat fading away, and 'hydrate' means to drink enough water
Q3. Charging customers eight times the ingredient cost for a simple dish is a very high ____.
markup liability dress code Show answermarkup — A 'markup' is the price increase from cost to retail; 'liability' is legal responsibility for harm, and 'dress code' is a clothing rule
Q4. A sign at the venue entrance explained the ____: no shorts, no open-toe shoes.
dress code regular liability Show answerdress code — A 'dress code' is an official rule about acceptable clothing; a 'regular' is a frequent customer, and 'liability' relates to legal responsibility
Q5. When jogging in summer heat, it is vital to ____ by drinking water every twenty minutes.
hydrate dissipate jerky Show answerhydrate — 'Hydrate' means to replenish the body's fluids; 'dissipate' describes something fading away (a smell, heat), and 'jerky' is a dried meat snack — a noun, not a verb
✍️ Mini Diary Today was quite an adventure. I went to try a new restaurant and got turned away at the entrance because I was wearing shorts — apparently they had a strict dress code. What annoyed me most was the double standard: several other guests inside were dressed just as casually as I was. The host kindly lent me a pair of plain trousers to wear inside, which was both embarrassing and oddly funny. By the time our wonderfully patient server brought us dessert, the whole silly experience had somehow managed to revive our faith in humanity.

The conversation wrapped up with a lively exchange about exercise habits and whether different activities really require different shoes.

Session Overview The session opened with the idiom ’take the reins’ and its literal roots in horsemanship, before moving into a wide-ranging discussion on time travel — whether to revisit the past or leap into the future, and which moments participants would change or simply witness. Learners shared personal reflections on career choices, childhood memories, advances in medicine, and the value of living in the present. The hour ended with a lively round of the card game Apples to Apples, which brought in fresh vocabulary such as ‘frazzled,’ ‘pathetic,’ and ‘casual.’
💬 Idioms “take the reins” to assume full control or authority over something, stepping into a leadership role
The new manager is taking the reins next week, so expect some changes. When the founder retired, her deputy took the reins and modernized the entire operation. “think outside the box” to approach a problem in a creative or unconventional way, going beyond the most obvious solutions
The engineering team was encouraged to think outside the box when the standard approach kept failing. Sometimes winning a word game means you have to think outside the box and make a surprising choice. “body is acting up” a part of your body (or a machine) is misbehaving or causing unexpected trouble
My knee has been acting up since I started running every morning. The photocopier was acting up all afternoon — it kept jamming mid-print. “pull on someone’s heartstrings” to cause a strong feeling of sympathy, tenderness, or sadness in someone
Reading her grandmother’s old handwritten recipes really pulled on her heartstrings. That documentary about elderly residents living alone pulled on everyone’s heartstrings. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember lifespan — the length of time a person, animal, or thing is expected to live or remain in use Advances in medicine have significantly increased the average human lifespan over the past century. frazzled — completely exhausted and stressed, usually from too much work or worry After back-to-back meetings all week, she arrived home looking completely frazzled. pathetic — deserving pity or contempt; very poor in quality or effort The team’s performance in the second half was pathetic — they barely touched the ball. holistic — dealing with the whole of something rather than only its individual parts The new curriculum takes a holistic approach, combining physical activity with academic learning. pivotal — of crucial importance; a turning point that strongly influences what comes next Choosing a field of study was a pivotal decision that shaped the rest of her career. hoarding — collecting or keeping large amounts of something, often selfishly, instead of sharing or using it Some people responded to the shortage by hoarding supplies they did not immediately need. casual — relaxed and unconcerned; also used for informal clothing or a laid-back attitude The office has a casual dress code on Fridays, so most people wear jeans. childbirth — the process and experience of giving birth to a baby Modern medical care has made childbirth much safer than it was a century ago. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ It’s good to me. ✅ It’s good for me. 💡 Use ‘for’ — not ’to’ — when describing something that benefits you: good for me, useful for me, helpful for me. ❌ Every king will get take the reins for their political philosophy. ✅ Every king would take the reins with their own political philosophy. 💡 Don’t add ‘get’ before a plain infinitive here; also use ‘would’ for hypothetical or habitual past statements. ❌ Nice meet. ✅ Nice to meet you. 💡 This fixed greeting requires the infinitive ’to meet’ plus the object ‘you’ — it is a set phrase and cannot be shortened. ❌ If I back to my younger period, I would like to study medicine. ✅ If I went back to my younger period, I would like to study medicine. 💡 In an unreal conditional, the if-clause needs a past-tense verb: ‘if I went back,’ not ‘if I back.’ ❌ The experience has teached me that many things don’t happen. ✅ Experience has taught me that most of the things I worried about never happen. 💡 ‘Teach’ is irregular — the past participle is ’taught,’ not ’teached.’ ❌ Future is so scared time. ✅ The future is such a scary time. 💡 Use ‘scary’ (describes the thing that causes fear) not ‘scared’ (describes how a person feels); also add the article ’the’ and use ‘such a’ for emphasis. ❌ Right span is more longer. ✅ Lifespan is getting longer. 💡 Never use ‘more’ with a one-syllable comparative — say ’longer,’ not ‘more longer.’ The correct word is also ’lifespan,’ not ‘right span.’ ❌ Instead of worry, you have to occupy. ✅ Instead of worrying, you have to keep yourself occupied. 💡 After ‘instead of,’ use a gerund (-ing form); the natural phrase for staying productive is ‘keep yourself occupied.’ ❌ I had the opportunity to discovered all the technologies. ✅ I had the opportunity to discover all the technologies. 💡 After ‘opportunity to,’ use the base infinitive form of the verb, not the past participle. ❌ I think this come from England. ✅ I think this came from England. 💡 The simple past of ‘come’ is ‘came’ — use the past tense when talking about something that happened in history. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. After three weeks of back-to-back deadlines, the project manager arrived at the meeting looking completely ____.
frazzled pathetic casual Show answerfrazzled — 'Frazzled' means exhausted and stressed from overwork; 'pathetic' implies something pitiable, and 'casual' means relaxed — the opposite of what an overworked manager would feel.
Q2. When the lead developer left the company, a junior team member ____ and delivered the product on schedule.
took the reins thought outside the box hoarding Show answertook the reins — 'Take the reins' means to step up and assume control; 'thought outside the box' describes creativity, and 'hoarding' means keeping things selfishly — neither describes taking over leadership.
Q3. Reading her late grandfather’s letters for the first time really ____ and she found herself in tears.
pulled on her heartstrings lifespan pivotal Show answerpulled on her heartstrings — 'Pull on someone's heartstrings' describes something that triggers deep emotion or tenderness; 'lifespan' is a noun about duration, and 'pivotal' is an adjective — neither works as a verb phrase expressing emotion.
Q4. Scientists believe that better nutrition and medical breakthroughs will extend the average human ____ well beyond 100 years.
lifespan childbirth hoarding Show answerlifespan — 'Lifespan' is how long a person lives, which fits perfectly; 'childbirth' is the act of having a baby, and 'hoarding' means collecting things excessively — neither describes the length of a life.
Q5. The standard approach wasn’t working, so the designer decided to ____ and came up with a completely unexpected solution.
think outside the box body’s acting up holistic Show answerthink outside the box — 'Think outside the box' means to find a creative, unconventional solution; 'body's acting up' describes a physical problem, and 'holistic' is an adjective — neither describes a creative action the designer took.
Q6. The clinic takes a ____ approach to patient care, treating the mind, body, and lifestyle together rather than just the symptoms.
holistic pivotal frazzled Show answerholistic — 'Holistic' means considering the whole rather than separate parts, which perfectly describes integrated care; 'pivotal' means a key turning point, and 'frazzled' means exhausted — neither fits as a description of a care philosophy.
✍️ Mini Diary Today I finally dragged myself to an evening language class at the community library, even though I was completely frazzled after an exhausting week. The instructor introduced the idiom ’take the reins,’ and before long we were deep in a discussion about time travel — whether we would go back to change a decision or leap into the future in search of better health and a longer lifespan. One participant quietly insisted that the present moment is the only one truly worth living, and I found that idea unexpectedly moving — it really pulled on my heartstrings. For me, the whole conversation was a pivotal reminder that real language learning happens through genuine exchange, not just textbook exercises. I walked home slowly, still turning over the question of where — or when — I would go if I ever got the chance.

Learners shared personal reflections on career choices, childhood memories, advances in medicine, and the value of living in the present. The hour ended with a lively round of the card game Apples to Apples, which brought in fresh vocabulary such as ‘frazzled,’ ‘pathetic,’ and ‘casual.’

content:
Session Overview The session opened with a participant demonstrating a self-built browser-based dictation app that reads sentences aloud and scores how accurately listeners can transcribe them, leading to a discussion of pronunciation tools and speech-recognition services. Conversation then shifted to regional accents — including Southern American and British varieties — and the challenge of tonal languages such as Mandarin, Cantonese, and Vietnamese. The group wrapped up by comparing tutoring cultures, school discipline practices, and university pathways across several countries, sharing personal stories of childhood independence and long language-learning journeys.
💬 Idioms “pick (something) up on the way out” to collect or take care of something as you leave a place, without making a special extra trip
She said she’d pick up the printed notes on her way out of the classroom. I’ll grab the package and pick it up on my way out of the building. “word by word” one word at a time, very slowly and carefully, without natural fluency
Before translation apps existed, he had to decode every foreign menu word by word. She read the legal contract word by word to make sure she understood every clause. “make a difference” to have a noticeable or important effect on something
Practising dictation every day really makes a difference to your listening accuracy. Living in a country where the language is spoken makes a huge difference to your fluency. “on purpose” done deliberately and intentionally, not by accident
The teacher made the listening sentences confusing on purpose to challenge the class. He used a different accent on purpose to test whether the speech app would still transcribe him correctly. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember dictation — a listening exercise in which you hear spoken words and write them down exactly as you hear them The dictation exercise revealed that she was mishearing certain vowel sounds. pronunciation — the way a word or language is spoken; how sounds are produced and combined The app let him record himself and compare his pronunciation with a model speaker. accuracy — how correct or error-free something is; often expressed as a percentage of right answers Her accuracy on the listening test was below sixty percent because the sentences were deliberately tricky. accent — a distinctive way of pronouncing a language, usually linked to a particular region or background After spending time abroad, she noticed her accent had gradually begun to shift. tongue twister — a phrase or sentence that is very difficult to say quickly because it contains similar or repeated sounds The teacher used a tongue twister to help students practise the difference between two sounds they kept confusing. tone — in linguistics, the pitch or musical quality on a syllable that changes its meaning — central to languages such as Mandarin, Cantonese, and Vietnamese In Mandarin, the same syllable can mean ‘mother’, ‘hemp’, or ‘horse’ depending on its tone. tutoring — extra private teaching given outside regular school hours, usually one-on-one or in a small group Many families pay for after-school tutoring to help their children prepare for entrance exams. connecting words — words or phrases (also called linking words or discourse markers) that join ideas and help speech or writing flow naturally, such as ‘however’, ’therefore’, or ’even though’ Learning connecting words made her spoken answers sound far more organised and natural. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ which songs you said is wrong ✅ which words you said were wrong 💡 The subject ‘words’ is plural, so the verb must be ‘were’, not ‘is’; ‘words’ (not ‘songs’) is also the intended meaning here. ❌ Is there a proof charging? / No free of charging. ✅ Is it free of charge? / No, there is no free charge. 💡 The fixed phrase is ‘free of charge’ — no article and no ‘-ing’ ending on ‘charge’. ❌ Today I remember. Tomorrow, I will forgot. ✅ Today I remember it, but tomorrow I will forget it. 💡 After a modal verb like ‘will’, always use the base form (‘forget’), not the past tense (‘forgot’). ❌ You believe me? (used to mean ‘do you have confidence in my ability to do this?’) ✅ Do you trust me? / Do you believe in me? 💡 ‘Believe someone’ means you think they are telling the truth; ’trust someone’ or ‘believe in someone’ expresses confidence in their ability or reliability. ❌ After I graduate, I throw out the book. ✅ After I graduated, I threw out the book. 💡 ‘Throw’ is irregular; its past tense is ’threw’. Use past tense throughout when telling a finished story. ❌ You must should do it. ✅ You should do it. 💡 English uses only one modal verb at a time; ‘must’ and ‘should’ cannot be combined. ❌ Some persons tell me. ✅ Some people told me. 💡 ‘People’ is the normal plural for humans in general conversation; ‘persons’ is very formal. Use past tense ’told’ when narrating past events. ❌ Why happened? ✅ Why did that happen? 💡 English questions need an auxiliary verb (‘did’) and a subject before the main verb. ❌ I was didn’t care about it. ✅ I didn’t care about it. 💡 Use either ‘was’ (for the verb ‘be’) or ‘didn’t’ (for a past negative action) — not both together. ❌ I don’t have so many choice to go to America. ✅ I didn’t have so many choices to go to America. 💡 ‘Choice’ is countable; after ‘so many’, use the plural ‘choices’. The past tense ‘didn’t have’ also fits the story context better. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. She recorded herself speaking and played it back to check her ____; she wanted to hear whether her sounds were correct.
pronunciation tutoring accent Show answerpronunciation — 'Pronunciation' is the specific way sounds are produced when speaking; 'tutoring' is extra teaching and 'accent' is a broader regional speech pattern — neither fits a sound-by-sound self-check.
Q2. The class repeated the difficult phrase over and over — it was a classic ____ designed to train the ear on two sounds that are easy to mix up.
tongue twister connecting words dictation Show answertongue twister — A 'tongue twister' is a phrase made hard to say quickly by repeated similar sounds; 'dictation' is a writing exercise and 'connecting words' are linking phrases — neither matches.
Q3. Committing to even ten minutes of focused listening practice every evening really ____.
makes a difference on purpose word by word Show answermakes a difference — 'Makes a difference' expresses a noticeable positive effect; 'on purpose' means deliberately and 'word by word' describes pace — neither completes the sentence naturally.
Q4. He admitted he had used a strong regional accent ____ to see whether the speech-recognition app would still understand him.
on purpose accuracy tone Show answeron purpose — 'On purpose' means deliberately or intentionally, which fits perfectly; 'accuracy' is a noun and 'tone' is a linguistic feature — neither works as an adverbial in this blank.
Q5. In Vietnamese, the same syllable can carry six completely different meanings because the language has six distinct ____s.
tone accent tutoring Show answertone — A 'tone' in linguistics is the pitch pattern on a syllable that changes a word's meaning; 'accent' is a regional speech style and 'tutoring' is extra teaching — neither fits the linguistic context.
Q6. Without a smartphone, she had to translate every sign ____, looking up each unfamiliar term one at a time in a paper dictionary.
word by word connecting words on purpose Show answerword by word — 'Word by word' means one word at a time, slowly and carefully; 'connecting words' are linking phrases and 'on purpose' means intentionally — neither describes the pace of translating.
✍️ Mini Diary Today in class, a participant demonstrated a self-built listening app — it plays a sentence aloud and asks you to type every word you hear. My accuracy turned out to be embarrassingly low; the sentences had been made confusing on purpose to expose the weak spots in our listening. I had especially struggled with the connecting words that stitch phrases together, which caused whole sentences to fall apart in my head. I grabbed the app link on my way out, determined to practise a little every evening before next week’s session.

The session opened with a participant demonstrating a self-built browser-based dictation app that reads sentences aloud and scores how accurately listeners can transcribe them, leading to a discussion of pronunciation tools and speech-recognition services. Conversation then shifted to regional accents — including Southern American and British varieties — and the challenge of tonal languages such as Mandarin, Cantonese, and Vietnamese. The group wrapped up by comparing tutoring cultures, school discipline practices, and university pathways across several countries, sharing personal stories of childhood independence and long language-learning journeys.

content:
Session Overview The session centered on a custom transcription tool one participant built to record class conversations and turn them into vocabulary lists and study notes on a public website. The group discussed whether sharing personal conversations with cloud-based AI services raised privacy and confidentiality concerns, and how consent should work in that setting. The conversation then broadened into a rich exploration of how people best learn languages — weighing technology and speed against immersion, real-life relationships, and lived experience.
💬 Idioms “weigh the pros and cons” to carefully think through the advantages and disadvantages of something before making a decision
Before joining any language-exchange app, it is worth taking time to weigh the pros and cons. The group weighed the pros and cons of sharing their class recordings before making a decision together. “at the click of a finger” instantly or with almost no effort; often used to describe how quickly technology can do something
With today’s AI tools, you can compile a list of phrasal verbs at the click of a finger. Information that once took days to find in a library is now available at the click of a finger. “live the language” to learn a language through real, everyday experiences and human relationships rather than just textbooks
Moving abroad and building friendships helped her truly live the language. You can study every grammar rule in the book, but you really have to live the language to sound natural. “mother tongue” the first language a person learned as a child; one’s native language
When he gets emotional in an argument, he always switches back to his mother tongue. She finds it easier to express complicated feelings in her mother tongue than in a second language. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember transcribe — to convert spoken words into written text The app automatically transcribes everything said in the meeting into a readable text file. consent — permission that someone gives freely and with full understanding Before recording the session, the organizer asked every participant for their consent. confidentiality — the practice of keeping personal or sensitive information private and not sharing it without permission The platform has strict confidentiality rules to protect the data its users share. nuance — a subtle difference in meaning, feeling, or tone that is not immediately obvious Even after years of study, grasping every nuance of a second language takes real-world practice. colloquial — belonging to informal, everyday spoken language rather than formal or written language The phrase ‘gonna’ is colloquial; in formal writing you would use ‘going to’. precaution — a careful action taken in advance to prevent a problem or reduce a risk As a precaution, the developer removed all names from the transcript before posting it online. immersion — surrounding yourself completely in a language or culture in order to learn it more naturally and quickly Total immersion in a new environment is one of the fastest ways to pick up a language. prompt engineering — the skill of writing clear, well-structured instructions to get the best results from an AI system Good prompt engineering can turn a vague AI response into something detailed and truly useful. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ There is many mistakes from me. ✅ I make many mistakes. 💡 Use ’there are’ with a plural noun (’there are many mistakes’); the simpler and more natural rewrite is ‘I make many mistakes’. ❌ If don’t use this tool, then I will change it in privately. ✅ If we don’t use this tool, I will change it privately. 💡 A subject is required before the verb (‘we don’t’); ‘in privately’ is incorrect — the adverb ‘privately’ stands alone with no preposition. ❌ I never thinking I can use it. ✅ I never thought I could use it. 💡 Use simple past (’thought’) and the past modal (‘could’) when describing what you believed at an earlier time. ❌ My husband don’t have time to bring me home. ✅ My husband doesn’t have time to take me. 💡 Third-person singular requires ‘doesn’t’; use ’take’ when moving someone away from the speaker, and ‘bring’ when moving toward the speaker. ❌ This application will develop by yourself. ✅ Did you develop this application yourself? 💡 The intended meaning is a question; mixing ‘will’ with a passive structure creates confusion — rephrase as a direct question in the simple past. ❌ I didn’t more effort to this. ✅ I didn’t put much effort into this. 💡 The natural collocation is ‘put effort into something’; the verb ‘put’ and the preposition ‘into’ are both required. ❌ I think learning language is not easy to quickly. ✅ I think learning a language too quickly is not easy. 💡 Add the article ‘a’ before a singular countable noun (‘a language’); move ’too quickly’ directly after what it modifies. ❌ Cannot easily denuance. ✅ You cannot easily grasp the nuance. 💡 ‘Denuance’ is not a real word; the correct noun is ’nuance’, and the natural phrase is ‘grasp the nuance’ or ‘pick up on the nuance’. ❌ I have a big disadvantage to compare English and Spanish. ✅ I have a big disadvantage when comparing English and Spanish. 💡 Use ‘when + -ing’ to describe a situation or circumstance; ’to compare’ sounds like a stated purpose rather than a condition. ❌ I found a podcast that an influence reunite more than 100 phrasal verbs. ✅ I found a podcast where an influencer compiled more than 100 phrasal verbs. 💡 Use ‘where’ for a source or place; the person is an ‘influencer’ (not ‘influence’); ‘compiled’ or ‘gathered’ fits better than ‘reunite’. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. She spent a long time trying to ____ before agreeing to let the class recordings go online.
weigh the pros and cons live the language at the click of a finger mother tongue Show answerweigh the pros and cons — This idiom means to think carefully about advantages and disadvantages before deciding; the other options describe language, speed, or origin — not a deliberation process.
Q2. He was concerned about the ____ of the personal stories people shared during the session.
confidentiality consent nuance immersion Show answerconfidentiality — 'Confidentiality' refers to keeping information private; 'consent' means giving permission, which is a different concept.
Q3. When she got upset, she always switched back to her ____ because she could express herself far more clearly.
mother tongue colloquial precaution prompt engineering Show answermother tongue — 'Mother tongue' is one's native first language; the other options are not types of language.
Q4. New translation software lets you convert a long article into another language ____.
at the click of a finger weigh the pros and cons immersion precaution Show answerat the click of a finger — This idiom means instantly or with almost no effort; the other options don't describe the speed or ease of completing a task.
Q5. She understood each word individually, but the ____ of the joke still escaped her.
nuance precaution colloquial consent Show answernuance — 'Nuance' means a subtle difference in meaning or tone; 'colloquial' describes an informal language style, not a quality of meaning.
Q6. She took every ____ to make sure no personal details appeared on the published website.
precaution consent immersion nuance Show answerprecaution — 'Take a precaution' is a natural collocation meaning to act carefully in advance to avoid a problem; 'consent' means giving permission, which doesn't fit the blank here.
✍️ Mini Diary Today I had a lot to think about after class. A classmate showed us a tool they had built that can transcribe our conversations and turn them into a study website — almost at the click of a finger. It sounded impressive, but I found myself quietly weighing the pros and cons: the vocabulary notes would be wonderful for review, yet some of what we share in class feels personal. In the end, we agreed to try it for just one session, and I left feeling that to really improve, you have to live the language — messy, human moments and all.

Session Overview

The session centered on a custom transcription tool one participant built to record class conversations and turn them into vocabulary lists and study notes on a public website. The group discussed whether sharing personal conversations with cloud-based AI services raised privacy and confidentiality concerns, and how consent should work in that setting. The conversation then broadened into a rich exploration of how people best learn languages — weighing technology and speed against immersion, real-life relationships, and lived experience.

content:
Session Overview The class began with tips for visiting a large university campus, then shifted into American history through a discussion of LBJ’s presidency and the Voting Rights Act of the 1960s. Participants explored the concept of southern hospitality and how it contrasts with the busier pace of life in large northern cities, briefly touching on the novel ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ as a cultural reference. The session closed with a lively comparison of online shopping platforms across several countries and a discussion of the advantages of visiting local farmer’s markets and independent shops in person.
💬 Idioms “southern hospitality” The tradition of exceptional warmth, friendliness, and generous welcome associated with people from the American South.
We felt real southern hospitality the moment we arrived — our hosts had cooked a full meal and stayed up talking with us until midnight. The small inn had a reputation for southern hospitality; every guest was greeted by name and offered homemade biscuits in the morning. “a gift for” A natural talent or special ability for a particular skill or activity.
She has a gift for languages and was already conversational in Korean after only six months of study. My grandfather had a gift for storytelling — he could turn a five-minute errand into an hour-long adventure. “pros and cons” The advantages (pros) and disadvantages (cons) of a choice or situation, weighed together.
We thought carefully about the pros and cons of ordering groceries online versus shopping at the market in person. There are pros and cons to living in a big city: plenty of opportunities, but also noise, traffic, and high prices. “slow-paced” Describes a lifestyle or environment that is relaxed, unhurried, and free from constant pressure.
After ten years in a crowded city, she was ready for the slow-paced life of a small town. The documentary showed a slow-paced village where neighbors still gathered on porches every evening just to talk. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember contemporary — A person who lived or worked during the same period as another; belonging to the same era. The civil rights leader and the president were contemporaries who sometimes worked toward the same goals. discriminate — To treat a person or group unfairly based on characteristics such as race, religion, or gender. The new law made it illegal to discriminate against any citizen when it came to the right to vote. notorious — Widely known for something negative or harmful. That stretch of highway was notorious for accidents caused by speeding drivers. autonomous — Having the right or power to govern itself independently, without full control from a larger authority. The region has an autonomous status, meaning it manages its own cultural and religious affairs locally. organic — Produced without artificial chemicals, synthetic fertilizers, or pesticides. Many shoppers willingly pay more for organic vegetables because they prefer food grown without chemicals. distribution center — A large warehouse where products are stored and then shipped out to customers. Because a distribution center opened nearby, online orders now arrive by the following morning. obey — To follow a rule, law, or instruction as required. Most drivers try to obey the speed limit, but on some highways many people go much faster. supply chain — The whole network of people, companies, and steps involved in getting a product from its origin to the customer. The global crisis disrupted the supply chain, causing delays and shortages of many everyday goods. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ the people is nice ✅ the people are nice 💡 ‘People’ is always plural in English, so the verb must be ‘are’, never ‘is’. ❌ I have fine several products that are cheaper in other places than Amazon ✅ I have found several products that are cheaper in other places than on Amazon 💡 The past participle of ‘find’ is ‘found’, not ‘fine’; also use ‘on Amazon’, not ‘in Amazon’. ❌ The delivered services is expensive ✅ The delivery service is expensive 💡 Use the noun ‘delivery’ (not the adjective ‘delivered’) to modify ‘service’; ‘service’ is singular here, so the verb is ‘is’. ❌ I not a member of Facebook ✅ I am not a member of Facebook 💡 English negation with ’not’ always requires the verb ’to be’: ‘I am not’, ‘she is not’, ’they are not’. ❌ I sell one of my car in Craig list ✅ I sold one of my cars on Craigslist 💡 Use past tense ‘sold’; ‘car’ must be plural after ‘one of my’; use the preposition ‘on’ with platform and website names. ❌ It depends. You want to are very interested in the history of Texas. ✅ It depends. If you are very interested in the history of Texas, it is a great choice. 💡 Use ‘if’ to introduce a condition; ‘you want to are’ is not grammatical — the conditional structure is simply ‘if you are’. ❌ some of Americans didn’t have right for support ✅ some Americans didn’t have the right to vote 💡 Do not add ‘of’ between ‘some’ and a noun; ‘right’ needs the article ’the’; the correct phrase is ’the right to vote’. ❌ I didn’t want to be lazy for order online ✅ I didn’t want to be lazy and just order online 💡 Use the conjunction ‘and’ (not the preposition ‘for’) to connect two related actions in one clause. ❌ Very struggling with the life ✅ People there really struggle with life 💡 ‘Very’ modifies adjectives and adverbs, not verbs; use ‘really struggle’ or ‘struggle a lot’ to add emphasis to a verb. ❌ I have visited Capitol ✅ I have visited the Capitol 💡 Unique, one-of-a-kind buildings and institutions take the definite article ’the’ — the Capitol, the White House, the Eiffel Tower. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. That town was once ____ for the unfair barriers it placed on certain groups of voters in the 1960s.
notorious autonomous contemporary Show answernotorious — 'Notorious' means widely known for something negative, which fits a place known for harmful voting policies; 'autonomous' means self-governing, and 'contemporary' means from the same time period — neither describes a bad reputation.
Q2. My colleague has ____ public speaking — she kept the entire audience engaged for over an hour.
a gift for southern hospitality pros and cons Show answera gift for — 'A gift for' expresses a natural talent for a specific skill; 'southern hospitality' is a cultural tradition of warmth, and 'pros and cons' refers to advantages and disadvantages — neither describes a personal ability.
Q3. We only buy ____ produce at the farmer’s market because we want food grown without pesticides or chemicals.
organic slow-paced notorious Show answerorganic — 'Organic' specifically describes food produced without artificial chemicals; 'slow-paced' describes a relaxed lifestyle, and 'notorious' means known for something bad — neither describes a farming method.
Q4. Before we decide, let’s think through the ____ of shopping online versus going to the store in person.
pros and cons supply chain autonomous Show answerpros and cons — 'Pros and cons' means the advantages and disadvantages of a choice, which fits a decision-making context; 'supply chain' is a business logistics term, and 'autonomous' means self-governing — neither fits weighing a personal choice.
Q5. Even though the speed limit was clearly posted, many drivers chose not to ____ it.
obey discriminate contemporary Show answerobey — 'Obey' means to follow a rule or law, which fits perfectly here; 'discriminate' means to treat someone unfairly based on a characteristic, and 'contemporary' is a noun/adjective meaning of the same era — neither fits following a traffic rule.
✍️ Mini Diary Today after class I decided to visit a local farmer’s market I had heard about, and from the moment I arrived I could feel the difference from my usual rushed errands. The whole place had a wonderfully slow-paced atmosphere — vendors leaned over their tables, chatted with every customer, and nobody seemed to be in any hurry at all. There was real southern hospitality in the air: one seller offered me a sample of honey even before I asked. I found some beautiful organic vegetables I had never seen before and spent a long time talking to the grower about how she raised them without any chemicals. Walking back to my car with a small jar of honey in hand, I thought about the pros and cons of always ordering online — it is certainly convenient, but I would have missed every bit of this.

Participants explored the concept of southern hospitality and how it contrasts with the busier pace of life in large northern cities, briefly touching on the novel ‘To Kill a Mockingbird’ as a cultural reference. The session closed with a lively comparison of online shopping platforms across several countries and a discussion of the advantages of visiting local farmer’s markets and independent shops in person.

Session Overview The class discussed how the US retirement system works, comparing social security, pensions, and 401(k) accounts. Learners also explored investment strategies including index funds, ETFs, and individual stocks, and discussed why most individual investors tend to underperform the broader market. The session ended with a conversation about compound interest, long-term holding strategies, and the emotional challenges of investing.
💬 Idioms “bump up” a sudden or noticeable increase in an amount or level
If you delay claiming your retirement benefit until age seventy, you receive a significant bump up in your monthly payment. After three years at the same company, she finally received a bump up in her salary. “get a head start” to begin something earlier than others, gaining an early advantage
Starting to save money in your twenties gives you a real head start on retirement. He arrived an hour early to get a head start on the day’s work. “on a roll” experiencing a continuous streak of success or good luck
After winning three hands in a row at the card table, he felt like he was on a roll. The company was on a roll, releasing two hit products in the same quarter. “diamond in the rough” a person or thing with great hidden potential that has not yet been fully developed or recognized
The coach saw the newcomer as a diamond in the rough and spent extra time training her. That overlooked stock turned out to be a diamond in the rough — its value quadrupled within three years. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember pension — a fixed regular payment made to a retired person by a former employer, guaranteed for life After thirty years of public service, he retired with a generous pension that covered all his basic expenses. 401(k) — a US employer-sponsored retirement savings account where the employee chooses how much to contribute and how to invest the money She increased her monthly contribution to her 401(k) so she would have a larger balance when she eventually retired. compound interest — interest calculated on both the original amount and the interest already earned, causing savings to grow faster over time Thanks to compound interest, the small deposit she made at age twenty had grown enormously by the time she reached retirement. contribute — to regularly put money into a savings or investment account He set up an automatic transfer to contribute a fixed amount to his retirement fund every month. tax-advantaged — describes an account or investment that offers special government tax benefits, such as reduced taxes on earnings Enrolling in a tax-advantaged savings plan can help your money grow faster because less of it goes to the government each year. diversify — to spread investments across different types of assets in order to reduce risk Rather than putting all her savings into one company, she chose to diversify across several industries. liquidate — to sell an investment and convert it into cash He had to liquidate part of his portfolio to pay for an unexpected expense. index fund — an investment fund designed to track the performance of a broad market index, offering wide exposure at low cost Instead of picking individual stocks, she put her savings into an index fund and did not touch it for fifteen years. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ Since I only were 16 years, I have a whole bunch of zeros. ✅ Since I only worked for 16 years, I have a whole bunch of zeros. 💡 Use the past verb ‘worked’ plus ‘for’ to describe a duration of employment; ‘were’ is a form of ‘be,’ not ‘work.’ ❌ 35 is very long period, right? ✅ 35 years is a very long period, right? 💡 State the unit (‘years’) and add the article ‘a’ before a singular countable noun such as ‘period.’ ❌ I must continue with the working. ✅ I must continue working. 💡 After ‘continue,’ use a gerund (verb + -ing) directly; ‘with the’ is not needed here. ❌ Only one stock is fail, I think. ✅ Only one stock has failed, I think. 💡 Use the present perfect (‘has failed’) to describe a past event whose result still matters now. ❌ Increasing is long time. Put down quickly. ✅ It takes a long time to go up, but it can drop very quickly. 💡 Each clause needs a clear subject (‘it’) and a complete verb phrase; avoid omitting both. ❌ Cannot endure the price down. ✅ I can’t endure the price going down. 💡 Include the subject ‘I’; after ’endure,’ use a gerund phrase (’the price going down’), not an adjective alone. ❌ My invest resort is minus 10% lost. ✅ My investment result is a 10% loss. 💡 ‘Investment’ is the noun form of ‘invest’; the correct word is ‘result,’ not ‘resort’; say ‘a 10% loss’ rather than ‘minus X% lost.’ ❌ It depends on person. ✅ It depends on the person. 💡 The expression ‘depend on’ requires ’the’ before a singular countable noun used in a general sense. ❌ I have worked for the IT field. ✅ I have worked in the IT field. 💡 Use ‘in’ for a field or industry; ‘for’ is reserved for a specific employer or organization. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. She decided to ____ her portfolio by putting money into stocks, bonds, and real estate instead of just one company.
liquidate diversify pension Show answerdiversify — 'Diversify' means to spread investments across different assets to reduce risk; 'liquidate' means to sell everything, and a 'pension' is a type of retirement payment — neither describes spreading investments.
Q2. His small deposit kept growing year after year because of ____ — the interest he earned began earning interest of its own.
compound interest pension index fund Show answercompound interest — 'Compound interest' describes the mechanism where returns earn further returns; a 'pension' and an 'index fund' are financial products, not growth mechanisms.
Q3. The sales team had closed a new deal every single day that week; they were clearly ____.
on a roll diamond in the rough get a head start Show answeron a roll — 'On a roll' describes a run of consecutive successes; 'diamond in the rough' refers to unrecognized potential, and 'get a head start' means to begin early — neither fits a winning streak.
Q4. By opening a retirement account right after graduation, she managed to ____ over classmates who waited until their thirties.
bump up on a roll get a head start Show answerget a head start — 'Get a head start' means to gain an early advantage; 'bump up' is a sudden increase in amount, and 'on a roll' describes ongoing success — neither captures starting earlier than others.
Q5. When the market crashed, he was forced to ____ his savings at a loss just to pay his monthly bills.
contribute liquidate compound interest Show answerliquidate — 'Liquidate' means to sell investments and turn them into cash; 'contribute' means to add money in, and 'compound interest' is a growth process — neither means selling off assets.
Q6. Enrolling in a ____ savings plan means a portion of your investment gains is sheltered from taxes each year.
tax-advantaged compound interest index fund Show answertax-advantaged — 'Tax-advantaged' describes the special tax treatment of an account; 'compound interest' is a growth mechanism, and 'index fund' is a type of investment product — neither describes a tax benefit.
✍️ Mini Diary After dinner tonight, I finally sat down to review my retirement savings — something I had been putting off for weeks. I was relieved to see that compound interest had quietly done its work: my balance had grown more than I expected simply by leaving it alone. I reminded myself how glad I was that I had chosen a tax-advantaged account years ago and decided to contribute a small fixed amount every month, even during tighter times. It felt good to know I had gotten a real head start on my future, instead of waiting until the pressure felt urgent.

Session Overview Participants shared personal stories about entrepreneurship, job dreams, and career paths — from reselling furniture in a shipping container to dreaming of a coffee cart. The group debated the pros and cons of working for large versus small companies, and discussed whether children should gain early business experience. The session also touched on workplace dress codes and how office attire has grown more casual over time.
💬 Idioms “get down to business” to stop chatting or delaying and start focusing on the real task at hand
We only have an hour for this meeting, so let’s get down to business. The teacher told the students to stop talking and get down to business. “ballpark figure” a rough, approximate estimate rather than an exact number
I don’t have the final cost yet, but a ballpark figure would be around three thousand dollars. Can you give me a ballpark figure for how long the renovation will take? “red tape” excessive bureaucratic rules, paperwork, or procedures that slow progress down
We wanted to open a small café, but there was so much red tape that it took a year just to get the permits. Starting a business abroad can be frustrating because of all the red tape involved. “not my cup of tea” something you do not enjoy or have no interest in
Managing a spreadsheet every day is not my cup of tea — I much prefer talking to people. She said that owning a business was not her cup of tea, but she deeply admired those who tried. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember savory — a flavor that is salty or meaty — the opposite of sweet I ordered a savory crepe filled with ham and cheese instead of the sweet chocolate one. mock interview — a practice job interview done before the real one, usually with a coach or a friend Doing a mock interview with her mentor helped her feel calm on the actual interview day. refurbish — to clean, repair, or improve an old object so it looks or works like new again He bought a damaged wooden chair at a thrift store and refurbished it over the weekend. resell — to sell something you have bought, usually at a higher price, in order to make a profit She finds branded clothes at garage sales and resells them online for a higher price. business-minded — naturally good at thinking about profit, strategy, and how to run a business Even as a student, he was very business-minded and was always looking for ways to earn extra money. incremental — happening in small, steady steps rather than all at once The company focused on incremental growth each year instead of trying to expand too fast. startup — a newly created business, often in technology, built around a new idea or product Most of her classmates had ideas for a startup, but she preferred to work for an established company first. dress code — a set of rules about what clothing is acceptable in a particular place or situation The office has a relaxed dress code, so most people wear jeans and casual shirts. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ I learns how to wax floors. ✅ I learned how to wax floors. 💡 Use simple past ’learned’ for a completed action; ’learns’ is third-person present singular and doesn’t match ‘I.’ ❌ You don’t have to be a rocket science. ✅ You don’t have to be a rocket scientist. 💡 The fixed expression refers to the person (‘rocket scientist’), not the field (‘rocket science’). ❌ We had to do a lot of kind of bread tape. ✅ We had to deal with a lot of red tape. 💡 The idiom is ‘red tape’ (bureaucratic obstacles), not ‘bread tape’; ‘deal with’ is the natural verb to pair with it. ❌ I firstly made a new site for TikTok time. ✅ I recently created a new website for Talk Time. 💡 ‘Firstly’ introduces the first item in a list; use ‘recently’ or ‘just’ to mean ’not long ago.’ ❌ I think maybe pass the 1st round. ✅ I think I may have passed the first round. 💡 The subject ‘I’ is missing, and ‘may have passed’ is needed to express uncertainty about something that happened in the past. ❌ It was surprised to me that all my classmates had startup ideas. ✅ I was surprised to find that all my classmates had startup ideas. 💡 The person feels the emotion, not the situation: say ‘I was surprised,’ not ‘it was surprised to me.’ ❌ Every person who have a business, he is a hero, for my opinion. ✅ Every person who has a business is a hero, in my opinion. 💡 Use ‘has’ after ‘who’ (singular); the subject already covers everyone, so no extra ‘he’ is needed; say ‘in my opinion,’ not ‘for my opinion.’ ❌ I do be late today. ✅ I was late today. 💡 ‘Do be’ is not used in standard English for simple statements; the simple past ‘was’ is correct here. ❌ My imaginal crepe is sweet one. ✅ The crepe I had imagined was a sweet one. 💡 ‘Imaginal’ is not a standard English word; use a relative clause like ’the crepe I had imagined’ instead. ❌ I apply for some other jobs like cashier or retail associate. ✅ I’m applying for some other jobs, like cashier or retail associate. 💡 Use the present progressive (‘I’m applying’) for an action that is in progress right now, not the simple present. ✅ Check Yourself Q1. We’ve been chatting for twenty minutes — it’s time to ____ and go over the budget.
get down to business ballpark figure not my cup of tea Show answerget down to business — 'Get down to business' means to stop socializing and focus on the task; a 'ballpark figure' is an estimate and 'not my cup of tea' expresses dislike — neither signals a shift in focus.
Q2. I haven’t counted all the receipts yet, but my ____ is around four hundred dollars.
ballpark figure dress code startup Show answerballpark figure — A 'ballpark figure' is an approximate number; 'dress code' refers to clothing rules and 'startup' to a new business — neither relates to giving an estimate.
Q3. Early morning meetings are really ____; I work much better in the afternoon.
not my cup of tea red tape ballpark figure Show answernot my cup of tea — 'Not my cup of tea' expresses that you dislike or have no interest in something; 'red tape' refers to bureaucracy and 'ballpark figure' to an estimate, so neither fits here.
Q4. Opening a food truck required so much ____ — permits, inspections, and endless forms.
red tape mock interview savory Show answerred tape — 'Red tape' describes frustrating bureaucratic obstacles; 'mock interview' is a practice interview and 'savory' is a flavor, so neither connects to permits and paperwork.
Q5. She asked a friend to help her with a ____ so she could practice answering tough questions.
mock interview dress code startup Show answermock interview — A 'mock interview' is a practice session before the real interview; 'dress code' relates to clothing rules and 'startup' to a new business — neither involves practicing answers.
Q6. The managers preferred ____ improvements each quarter over trying to double the company in one year.
incremental savory business-minded Show answerincremental — 'Incremental' describes small, gradual steps forward; 'savory' describes taste and 'business-minded' describes a type of person — neither fits the idea of measured growth.
✍️ Mini Diary Today I walked past a small shop near my neighborhood and spotted a scratched-up wooden chair in the window. The owner told me she likes to refurbish old furniture and resell it online — something I had never thought of trying myself. I nearly spent an hour just chatting with her, but eventually reminded myself to get down to business and ask the real question: how much for the chair? She couldn’t name an exact price on the spot, but offered a ballpark figure of about forty dollars. I paid, thanked her, and carried the chair home, already imagining how good it would look beside my desk.

Session Overview The class explored US coins and bills, focusing on how Americans write and say numbers — especially the difference between using a period as a decimal mark versus a comma as a thousands separator. Learners then compared payment habits in their home countries, discussing tap to pay, QR codes, Venmo, and even government-backed digital currencies. The session ended with a creative shop-building activity to practice writing prices and a round of the vocabulary card game Apples to Apples.
💬 Idioms “apples to apples” Comparing two things that are alike and in the same category; the opposite, ‘apples to oranges,’ means comparing things that are too different to be fairly compared
Before choosing a phone plan, compare apples to apples — make sure both options include the same data limit. Saying a bicycle is slower than a plane is apples to oranges; they serve completely different purposes. “bad apple” One dishonest or troublesome person in an otherwise good group, who risks negatively influencing the others
Most of the staff is reliable, but one bad apple keeps calling in sick on busy weekends. The coach said one bad apple on the team was spreading a negative attitude before every game. “hardly worth anything” Having almost no monetary or practical value; not worth the cost or effort
The US penny is hardly worth anything now — it costs more to produce than its face value. After sitting in the garage for fifteen years, the old exercise bike was hardly worth anything. 📚 Vocabulary to Remember denomination — The official face value printed on a coin or banknote, such as $1, $5, or $20 The cashier asked if I wanted my change in small denominations so I could use it at the parking meter. counterfeit — Fake money (or goods) made to look like the real thing in order to deceive people The store uses a special pen to check whether large bills are counterfeit before accepting them. decimal mark — The punctuation symbol that separates a whole number from its fractional part; in the US, a period (.) is used, so $3.75 means three dollars and seventy-five cents In the US, the decimal mark is a period, so 3.75 means three dollars and seventy-five cents, not three thousand and seventy-five. in circulation — Actively being used and passed around in the economy; not stored away or taken out of use The US Mint stopped making new pennies, so only the coins already in circulation will remain. cover fee — An entrance charge you pay at the door of a bar, club, or event, separate from anything you buy inside The venue charges a $10 cover fee on Friday nights, so it is a good idea to bring cash. tap to pay — A contactless payment method where you hold your phone or credit card near a reader to complete a purchase without swiping or inserting a card I left my wallet at home, but I was still able to use tap to pay with my phone to buy lunch. enunciate — To pronounce each word clearly and distinctly so the listener can easily understand Language teachers tend to enunciate more carefully in class than they do in everyday conversation. heirloom — A valuable or meaningful object that has been passed down from one generation to the next within a family My grandmother’s gold watch is a family heirloom that will one day belong to my daughter. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ She don’t know who this is. ✅ She doesn’t know who this is. 💡 Third-person singular subjects (he / she / it) require ‘doesn’t,’ not ‘don’t.’ ❌ I have one year here and I never use any of the cash. ✅ I have been here for one year and I have never used any cash. 💡 Use the present perfect (‘have been,’ ‘have used’) for situations that started in the past and continue up to now. ❌ My wife don’t like to meet Korean people. ✅ My wife doesn’t like to meet Korean people. 💡 Third-person singular subjects need ‘doesn’t’ in negative sentences. ❌ But didn’t use any Korean languaging. ✅ But they didn’t use any Korean. 💡 ‘Languaging’ is not a standard English word; the sentence also needs a subject (’they’) to be complete. ❌ And the 1st time, I cannot catch it. ✅ The first time, I couldn’t catch it. 💡 Use ‘couldn’t’ (past tense of ‘can’t’) when describing a past inability; ‘cannot’ is present tense. ❌ It’s very difficult to understand native speakers, speed, speaking speed. ✅ It is very difficult to understand native speakers’ speaking speed. 💡 Use the possessive apostrophe (‘speakers’’) to show that the speed belongs to the speakers. ❌ Sometimes I’m eating the word, I think, omitting the word. ✅ Sometimes I think I’m dropping or omitting words. 💡 ‘Eating a word’ is not standard English; ‘dropping a word’ or ‘omitting a word’ expresses the idea naturally. ❌ There is some other means to paint with the coin. ✅ There are some other ways to pay with currency. 💡 ‘Means’ used as a plural noun takes ‘are’; ‘paint’ appears to be a mishearing of ‘pay’; ‘currency’ is clearer than ‘coin’ here. ❌ In my phone, one app downloaded, they pay this app for money. ✅ On my phone, I downloaded an app that I use to pay. 💡 Use ‘on’ with devices (‘on my phone’); the sentence needs a clear subject (‘I’) and a relative clause to connect the ideas. ❌ Sometime I bought Facebook Marketplace, sometimes people says only he accepted cash. ✅ Sometimes on Facebook Marketplace, people say they only accept cash. 💡 ‘Sometimes’ (not ‘sometime’) for repeated events; ‘people say’ needs no -s; use ’they’ not ‘he’ when referring back to ‘people.’ ✅ Check Yourself Q1. The US penny is ____ — it costs more to produce than it is worth, which is why the Mint has stopped making new ones.
hardly worth anything in circulation counterfeit Show answerhardly worth anything — 'Hardly worth anything' means having almost no value; 'in circulation' describes active use, and 'counterfeit' means fake — neither describes low monetary worth.
Q2. Before the cashier accepted the $100 bill, she held it up to the light to make sure it was not ____.
counterfeit heirloom denomination Show answercounterfeit — 'Counterfeit' means fake money made to deceive; 'heirloom' is a cherished family object, and 'denomination' is a bill's face value — neither matches 'fake.'
Q3. In the US, the ____ separates dollars from cents, so $4.99 means four dollars and ninety-nine cents, not four thousand and ninety-nine.
decimal mark cover fee denomination Show answerdecimal mark — 'Decimal mark' is the period (.) between dollars and cents; 'cover fee' is an entrance charge, and 'denomination' is a bill's face value.
Q4. The old wooden clock on the mantle is a family ____ that has been passed down for over a hundred years.
heirloom cover fee bad apple Show answerheirloom — 'Heirloom' means an object passed through generations; 'cover fee' is an entrance charge, and 'bad apple' describes a troublesome person — neither fits.
Q5. The bar charges a $5 ____ on weekend nights, so the host reminded everyone to bring a little cash.
cover fee tap to pay denomination Show answercover fee — 'Cover fee' is the charge paid at the door to enter a venue; 'tap to pay' is a payment method, and 'denomination' is a bill's value — neither names an entrance charge.
Q6. When you shop for apartments, be sure you are comparing ____: check that both listings include utilities in the monthly rent.
apples to apples hardly worth anything in circulation Show answerapples to apples — 'Apples to apples' means comparing like with like; 'hardly worth anything' describes low value, and 'in circulation' describes active use — neither fits a comparison context.
✍️ Mini Diary This morning I finally made it to the Saturday farmers market downtown, something I had been putting off for weeks. Most stalls only accepted cash, and the loose coins rattling in my pocket were hardly worth anything — not nearly enough for even the smallest item. I had to find an ATM first, which cost me twenty minutes and a little embarrassment. Once I had bills in hand, I picked up a jar of local honey for $8.50, and I double-checked the decimal mark on the price card so I wouldn’t confuse dollars and cents the way I sometimes still do. Near the exit, a jewellery stall caught my eye; the maker explained that each piece was crafted to become a family heirloom, designed to be worn and passed on for generations. I spent more than I planned, but I walked home with a full bag and no regrets.

Learners then compared payment habits in their home countries, discussing tap to pay, QR codes, Venmo, and even government-backed digital currencies. The session ended with a creative shop-building activity to practice writing prices and a round of the vocabulary card game Apples to Apples.

Session Overview The class opened with a moral dilemma about choosing between two bad options, introducing the idiom ‘between a rock and a hard place.’ Learners then shared personal stories about driving as teenagers in Mexico, exploring Austin’s parks, and kayaking on Lake Travis, comparing outdoor culture and nighttime safety across South Korea, China, and the United States. One learner described a month-long solo Amtrak journey from San Diego through Chicago and back to Austin, sparking discussion about train passes, senior discounts, and spontaneous travel.
💬 Idioms “between a rock and a hard place” Stuck in a situation where every available choice leads to a bad result; forced to pick between two difficult options.
She was between a rock and a hard place: cancel the flight and lose the money, or travel while sick. The small restaurant was between a rock and a hard place — raise prices and lose regulars, or keep prices and go broke. “on and off” Not continuously; sometimes happening and sometimes not, in an irregular or inconsistent pattern.
We have been talking about moving to a bigger apartment on and off for two years without ever deciding. The internet connection was on and off all morning, so the video call kept cutting out. “bad apple” One person in a group who causes trouble or has a negative effect on everyone else — from the idea that a single rotten apple can spoil an entire barrel.
Most of the students were engaged and polite; there was just one bad apple who kept interrupting. The coach reminded everyone before the tournament: ‘We are a team — don’t be the bad apple.’ 📚 Vocabulary to Remember consequence — A result or effect — often negative — that follows from a decision or action. Ignoring a small car problem now can have serious consequences later. conditions — The specific rules or requirements that must be followed as part of an agreement or offer. Before signing the lease, read all the conditions so you know what is expected of you. within — Before a time limit ends; inside a specified period. You must use the promotional code within 14 days of receiving it. shade — An area protected from direct sunlight, making it feel cooler. On a hot day, the children moved their game to the shade of a large tree. humid — Describing air that contains a high level of moisture, making hot weather feel even more uncomfortable. August in Austin is extremely humid, so even a short walk outside leaves you sweating. register — To officially record something — a vehicle, a product, or yourself — with an authority or organization. You need to register your boat before you can legally launch it on a public lake. paddle — A flat-bladed pole used to propel a small boat through water; also a verb meaning to move a boat this way. We took turns to paddle the canoe upstream against the slow current. debt — An amount of money that you owe to another person or organization. She worked extra shifts every weekend to pay off her credit-card debt. 🔧 Say It Better ❌ We used to kayaking. ✅ We used to go kayaking. 💡 ‘Used to’ must be followed by a base verb, not a gerund (-ing form). The correct pattern is ‘used to go kayaking.’ ❌ In the May, I go there. ✅ In May, I went there. 💡 Month names never take the article ’the.’ Also use past tense (‘went’) for a completed past action. ❌ Some places is permitted to kayak. ✅ Kayaking is permitted in some places. 💡 The grammatical subject should be the activity (‘kayaking’), not ‘places.’ Add the preposition ‘in’ before ‘some places.’ ❌ I also traveled it by myself. ✅ I also traveled by myself. 💡 ‘Travel’ is intransitive and cannot take a direct object — simply remove ‘it.’ ❌ So I’m not have the 30 days. ✅ So I didn’t have the full 30 days. 💡 Past tense negation requires ‘didn’t + base verb.’ The form ‘I’m not have’ incorrectly mixes present and past structures. ❌ The last month I go to the California, the seaside. ✅ Last month I went to California, to the seaside. 💡 Time expressions like ’last month’ take no article. State and country names take no ’the’ (with a few exceptions). Use past tense for a completed trip. ❌ At 15, but with a sign letter of your parents. ✅ At 15, but with a signed letter from your parents. 💡 ‘Signed’ (past participle as adjective) means the letter carries a signature. Also use ‘from,’ not ‘of,’ when indicating the source of a document. ❌ Because of the heart, in the summer. ✅ Because of the heat in the summer. 💡 ‘Heat’ (high temperature) and ‘heart’ (the organ) sound very similar. When talking about uncomfortable weather, the word you need is ‘heat.’ ❌ He’s clean a rock and a hard place. ✅ It’s a real rock-and-a-hard-place situation. 💡 The full idiom is ‘between a rock and a hard place.’ The key preposition is ‘between,’ and the whole phrase is fixed — avoid substituting or rearranging its words. ❌ My parents, authorization, or concept, or… 15 is possible in Mexico. ✅ With my parents’ consent — or authorization — you can get a license at 15 in Mexico. 💡 ‘Consent’ means agreement or permission; ‘concept’ means an abstract idea. They sound similar but have very different meanings — for permission, use ‘consent’ or ‘authorization.’ ✅ Check Yourself Q1. My boss needs me to work this Saturday, but I already promised my children a day out — I’m really ____.
between a rock and a hard place on and off bad apple Show answerbetween a rock and a hard place — Both choices lead to a bad outcome (disappointing the boss or the children), which is exactly what 'between a rock and a hard place' describes. 'On and off' describes frequency and 'bad apple' describes a troublesome person — neither fits a dilemma.
Q2. She practices piano ____, sometimes every day and sometimes not at all, so her progress is slow.
on and off within bad apple Show answeron and off — 'On and off' describes an irregular, inconsistent pattern over time. 'Within' sets a time deadline and 'bad apple' refers to a troublesome person — neither fits the idea of inconsistent practice.
Q3. If your kayak has a motor, you are legally required to ____ it with the state water authority before launching.
register paddle shade Show answerregister — 'Register' means to officially record a vehicle with an authority. 'Paddle' is a movement verb and 'shade' refers to shelter from sunlight — neither belongs in a legal registration sentence.
Q4. Please review all the ____ of the membership before you pay, especially the cancellation policy.
conditions debt consequence Show answerconditions — 'Conditions' are the specific rules or terms of an agreement. 'Debt' is money owed and 'consequence' is the result of an action — neither describes the terms of a membership plan.
Q5. All applications must be submitted ____ 30 days of the original purchase date.
within humid on and off Show answerwithin — 'Within' introduces a time boundary ('before 30 days are up'). 'Humid' is a weather adjective and 'on and off' describes frequency — neither fits a deadline sentence.
Q6. He borrowed money every month for a year and is now struggling to repay his ____.
debt shade consequence Show answerdebt — 'Debt' is the money owed after borrowing. You 'repay' a debt; you cannot 'repay shade' (shelter from sun) or 'repay a consequence' (a result) — those combinations make no sense.
✍️ Mini Diary Last Saturday I woke up early and headed to a riverside park to beat the humid summer heat before the crowds arrived. I found a bench under some old oak trees where the shade made the morning feel almost comfortable, and I sat watching a family carry their kayak down to the water’s edge. For a moment I was between a rock and a hard place: I desperately wanted to join them on the water, but I hadn’t registered my own kayak with the city yet and didn’t want to risk a fine. I decided to simply walk along the bank instead, listening to the soft sound of paddles pushing through the river. It turned out to be exactly the quiet morning I needed.

Session Overview

The class opened with a moral dilemma about choosing between two bad options, introducing the idiom ‘between a rock and a hard place.’ Learners then shared personal stories about driving as teenagers in Mexico, exploring Austin’s parks, and kayaking on Lake Travis, comparing outdoor culture and nighttime safety across South Korea, China, and the United States. One learner described a month-long solo Amtrak journey from San Diego through Chicago and back to Austin, sparking discussion about train passes, senior discounts, and spontaneous travel.
